themes.name: Medieval Europe
themes.strapline: Walls, guilds and the towns that stopped changing
themes.summary: A medieval town survives for one of two reasons: it stayed poor, or it stayed useful. These did one or the other. Look for the shape rather than the set pieces — a market square where the roads meet, a wall that a rich century paid for, and a church larger than the population ever justified.

stops.why: Rich in 1400, silted up by 1500, and preserved by five centuries of not mattering.
A city that lost to Florence and was frozen by losing; the Palio still runs on the old rivalries.
The most complete town wall in northern Europe, with twenty towers still standing.
A Saxon citadel in Transylvania, still lived in rather than staged.
Roman, Viking and medieval in one square mile, walkable on the walls.
The largest inhabited medieval town in Europe, built by crusader knights.
Gothic on a scale nothing else north of the Alps managed, and never bombed.
Venetian walls climbing 260 metres up a cliff behind a walled town.

themes.name: Sacred Europe
themes.strapline: Where people have gone on purpose for a thousand years
themes.summary: Pilgrimage built more of Europe than any king did: the roads, the bridges, the hostels, the towns that grew where walkers stopped. These places span four Christian traditions and are all still in use — which means visiting them means visiting somebody's church rather than a monument.

stops.why: The end of the Camino, where people still arrive on foot every afternoon.
The smallest state in the world and the largest church in it.
A murder in 1170 made this the most walked-to place in medieval England.
Six monasteries on sandstone pillars, once reached only by rope and net.
Bulgaria's fortified monastery, which kept the language alive under Ottoman rule.
White marble and frescoes from 1209, in a Serbian valley with nothing else in it.
A 6th-century monastic city in a Wicklow valley with two lakes.
A monastery carved into the rock face, where singers use the stone as the instrument.

themes.name: Viking Europe
themes.strapline: Ships, settlements and the places they reached
themes.summary: The Norse were traders and settlers more often than raiders, and the archaeology says so: ships built for cargo, parliaments held in the open air, and towns founded from Dublin to Kyiv. These are the places where you can see the evidence rather than the reputation.

stops.why: Five ships scuttled to block a fjord in 1070, raised whole and reconstructed.
Where the Icelandic Althing met in the open air from 930 — a parliament in a rift valley.
The cod that funded the whole thing, still dried on racks every spring.
The polar and Viking ship collections, and the fjord they were built for.
Normandy: Norse settlers within a century of arriving, and the embroidery that records what they did next.
Founded as a Norse longphort in 841, and the excavations under the modern city.
Jorvik: the Danish capital of northern England for nearly a century.
The Settlement Exhibition, built around a 10th-century longhouse found under the street.

themes.name: Mountain Europe
themes.summary: Europe's mountains are not one thing. The Alps are high and serviced; the Caucasus is higher and barely; the Tatras are compressed; the Picos end in the sea; the Accursed Mountains have a blood-feud memory and a trail through three countries. This is the case for treating them as different places rather than one activity.

stops.why: The Alps at their most vertical, and the birthplace of the sport.
Cliff-shelf villages reachable only by cable car, under the Eiger.
The Dolomites: pale limestone towers over meadows, with wartime via ferrata still bolted in.
Poland's only alpine range, compressed into a few valleys and thoroughly loved.
The Caucasus, higher than the Alps, with defensive towers in every village.
Limestone peaks twenty kilometres from the Atlantic, with cheese aged in the caves.
Durmitor's plateau and the second-deepest canyon in the world.
The Accursed Mountains, and a six-hour pass between two valleys that had no road.

themes.name: Roman Europe
themes.strapline: The empire, where it is still standing up
themes.summary: Rome's best surviving buildings are mostly not in Rome. They are in the provinces, where a later city did not need the stone, or where a cathedral was built inside the temple instead of on top of it. These are the places where the engineering is still doing its job.

stops.why: The Pantheon's dome: still the largest unreinforced concrete span ever built.
An amphitheatre from 90 AD that is still used for events.
A retirement palace that became a town and never stopped being lived in.
Ephesus: the library facade, the marble street and the terrace-house mosaics.
The only hot spring in Britain, plumbed by Romans and still running through their lead.
A theatre for 6,000, rediscovered by a landslide in 1972 and back in use.
Greek first, then Roman, with the temple columns embedded in the cathedral wall.
Cyprus's museums hold the province's mosaics; Paphos has them still on the floor.

themes.name: Wine Europe
themes.strapline: Eight regions that do not taste like each other
themes.summary: The interesting wine map of Europe is not the famous one. It includes clay vessels buried in Georgian courtyards, volcanic vines woven into baskets against Aegean wind, and slate slopes on the Rhine at sixty degrees. Every one of these places will let you taste in the cellar where it was made.

stops.why: The reference point, and Saint-Émilion's small growers behind it.
Burgundy's slope, where the parcels have names and the walls are older than the borders.
The Douro: schist terraces too steep for machines, and treading still done by foot.
The first classified region in the world, from 1737, in cellars furred with black mould.
Georgia: eight thousand years of fermenting in buried qvevri, skins and all.
Moravia at harvest, when half-fermented burčák appears for three weeks and then vanishes.
Assyrtiko from vines trained into wreaths on the ground against the wind.
The Rhine gorge, where the good slopes are steep enough to need a winch.

themes.name: Rail Europe
themes.strapline: Journeys where the train is the destination
themes.summary: Some lines were built to move slate, ore or salt and are now worth the fare on their own. Others were engineering arguments. All of these are scheduled public services rather than tourist excursions, which means you can use them as transport and get the spectacle for the price of a ticket.

stops.why: 865 metres of descent in twenty kilometres, and a gravel road to ride back down.
The Bernina line: glacier to palm trees in four hours, over a UNESCO-listed railway.
The Rhine gorge line, forty castles in sixty-five kilometres, on an ordinary regional train.
The Šargan Eight: a narrow-gauge line that loops over itself to climb.
Slate railways built to run downhill by gravity, now running for the view.
The Douro line, hugging the water past terraces the whole way.
The Iron Ore Line to the Norwegian coast, through Lapland and above the tree line.
Cog railways and cable cars as public transport, timed to the minute.

themes.name: Island Europe
themes.strapline: Where the ferry timetable is the itinerary
themes.summary: An island changes the pace before you arrive, because you have to wait for a boat. These eight are chosen for being genuinely themselves rather than resort annexes — a Baltic sand spit, a Hebridean distillery island, an Adriatic island closed to outsiders until 1989, and a Cycladic island that farms.

stops.why: The Cyclades' agricultural heart: mountain villages, marble quarries and long beaches.
Closed as a military base until 1989 and undeveloped because of it.
Irish as a daily language, 1,600 km of dry stone wall, and a fort on an 87-metre cliff.
Dutch Wadden: dunes, seals, and mudflats you can walk across at low tide.
Nine distilleries, 3,000 people, and 50,000 wintering geese.
Malta's slower sister, with temples older than the pyramids.
A sand spit shared with Russia, where the dunes buried four villages.
Granite peaks straight out of the Norwegian Sea, above red fishing cabins.

themes.name: Jewish Europe
themes.strapline: A thousand years, and what remains of it
themes.summary: Jewish communities shaped European cities for a millennium before most of them were destroyed in the twentieth century. These places hold both halves of that: living communities and institutions, and the sites of what happened. They are visited best slowly, with the museums that were built by the communities themselves rather than about them.

stops.why: Kazimierz: seven synagogues in a district that is a neighbourhood again, and Auschwitz an hour away.
Six synagogues and a cemetery with twelve layers of graves, preserved by a terrible irony.
Synagogues built by Muslim craftsmen for Jewish congregations under Christian kings.
A city that was majority Sephardic until 1943; the museum tells it without flinching.
The 'Jerusalem of the North', and the Gaon's city, almost entirely erased in 1941–44.
One of Europe's best-preserved medieval Jewish quarters, with a museum in it.
POLIN, which spends most of its space on a thousand years of life rather than its ending.
A Moravian rabbinical seat, with a hillside cemetery of four thousand graves.

themes.name: Renaissance Europe
themes.summary: The Renaissance happened where banking did, and the buildings are the receipts. These are the city states that funded it and the courts that competed with them — plus the two places that exported the style north and made it something else.

stops.why: Banking money, and nearly all of it inside a twenty-minute walk.
The rival that lost, and was preserved by losing.
A republic that bought its art from everywhere and kept it.
Where the popes outspent the bankers, and Michelangelo worked for both.
The oldest university in the world, and the arcades built to keep scholars dry.
Leonardo's last house, and the château where the style crossed the Alps.
The Isenheim altarpiece: what the north did with the same century.
Rubens's own house and studio, in the city that took Venice's trade.

themes.name: The Grand Tour
themes.summary: For two hundred years a wealthy young northern European was sent south to learn taste, and the itinerary barely changed: Paris, the Alps, the Italian cities, ideally Greece. The route survives, the coaching inns are hotels, and the trains do in hours what took them weeks.

stops.why: The first stop, then as now, and the one that taught manners rather than antiquity.
The Alps, which the eighteenth century found terrifying and the nineteenth found sublime.
Over the pass and into Italy: the first opera house of the journey.
Carnival, Canaletto, and the paintings they took home as souvenirs.
The Uffizi, already a public gallery when the tourists arrived.
The point of the whole thing, and where the drawings were made.
Vesuvius, Pompeii newly dug, and the furthest most of them got.
The few who kept going, and came back with the Parthenon in their sketchbooks.

themes.name: Thermal Europe
themes.summary: Europe sits on hot water in more places than people realise, and every culture that found some built something around it: Roman baths, Ottoman hammams, Habsburg spa towns, Icelandic municipal pools and a Finnish sauna in every building. Bathing is the oldest continuous European leisure activity there is.

stops.why: The only hot spring in Britain, plumbed by Romans and still running through their lead.
A hundred springs under one city, and outdoor pools that are better in the snow.
Neighbourhood geothermal pools, which is where Reykjavík actually socialises.
Public saunas returned to the waterfront, and the Baltic to jump into.
Balkan mountain spa water, at a tenth of Alpine prices.
Not thermal but geological: fire that comes out of the ground and has for millennia.
Sulphur baths under brick domes, an hour that costs less than a meal.
Not a spa: glacial water, and the point is how cold it is.

themes.name: Modernist Europe
themes.summary: Between about 1920 and 1975 Europe rebuilt itself twice and argued about how the whole time. These are the places where the argument is still standing: social housing that worked, a manifesto in a house, a city rebuilt from nothing, and one that decided not to be rebuilt at all.

stops.why: Flattened in 1940 and rebuilt as an argument that the past is owed nothing.
Red Vienna's housing: Karl-Marx-Hof is a kilometre long and people still live in it.
Rietveld's Schröder House — De Stijl as a building rather than a painting.
Every phase of it, including the parts that were built to face each other.
Rebuilt from eighteenth-century paintings, then given a Stalinist tower.
One monumental avenue, planned whole, and unusually complete as a piece of design.
Villa Tugendhat, 1930, and the reason people book months ahead.
Rebuilt in concrete after 1963, then rebuilt again in marble, and argued about daily.
